paper.title: Vocational versus General Upper Secondary Education and Earnings
paper.code_data_availability: 'This paper uses administrative data from Statistics Denmark that are not publicly available due to data protection laws. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish administrative data (Statistics Denmark); the paper refers to 'registers' collectively and names no individual register
registers.years: cohorts born 1986-89 followed until 2018; 9th grade test score information available from 2002
registers.role: outcomes / treatment / controls / linkage / sample frame
variables_mentioned: teachers' marks for the year's work

registers.name_in_paper: Danish administrative registers for the older cohorts born 1974-1977 (the 'old sample' used to fit the surrogate index)
registers.role: estimation of the surrogate index used to predict earnings at age 40
variables_mentioned: educational attainment (290 indicators based on the Danish version of ISCED)
GPA from general upper secondary school

registers.name_in_paper: Geographic co-ordinates of educational institutions and of the 100 x 100 metre quadrant containing the student's residence (road-network distances)
registers.years: measured January 1st in the year the student leaves lower secondary school (typically at age 15)
variables_mentioned: distance to the seven main vocational education tracks
distance to the four main general education tracks

linkages: Unique personal identification numbers make it possible to link different registers
The data contain links between children and parents, used for parental background controls
Students' residential addresses (south-west corner of the 100 x 100 metre quadrant) linked to the exact geographic co-ordinates of educational institutions via road-network distances
Main sample (cohorts 1986-89) linked to an 'old sample' (cohorts 1974-77) through a common surrogate-index prediction model

sample.universe: Individuals from the 1986-1989 birth cohorts who were enrolled in Danish lower secondary schools
selection_rules: Born 1986-89 (the first four cohorts for which 9th grade test score information exists)
Enrolled in Danish lower secondary schools
Completed an upper secondary education program by age 25
Living in Denmark the year they left lower secondary school, at age 25, and in the years in which outcomes are measured
Information on distance to educational institutions available (distances are not calculated for students living on small islands without a bridge to the mainland)
Earnings at age 28 trimmed if negative or above DKK 1m ($153,800) -- less than 0.4% of the sample
Analysis conducted separately for males (N = 79,070) and females (N = 82,362)
sample.period: 9th grade typically completed in 2002-2005; registers followed until 2018

construction_notes: Treatment status is defined by the first completed program for students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25

Earnings = annual wage income plus income from self-employment, before taxes, deflated by the consumer price index with base year 2015, measured in USD 1,000 at the end-2018 exchange rate $1 = DKK 6.5
Earnings at age 28 are trimmed if negative or above DKK 1m ($153,800)

Predicted earnings at age 40 is a surrogate index: four OLS models (one per cohort, conditioning on short-term outcomes by age 28, 29, 30 and 31) estimated on cohorts 1974-77, each with about 890 parameters and about 260,000 observations, adjusted R-squared 0.43-0.50
Educational attainment in the surrogate model is measured by 290 indicator variables based on the Danish version of ISCED, combining level and narrowly defined field of study

Distance instruments are weighted average road-network distances to the seven main vocational tracks and the four main general tracks, weighted by the overall number of students choosing each main track; the two distance variables correlate 0.81
Controls: 3 cohort dummies, 92 municipality of residence dummies, and 62 family background and 9th grade test score variables (Online Appendix Table A5)
Low / medium / high 9th grade math score groups are defined by the average of the math test score and the teacher's mark for the year's work (<=7, 7-9, >=9), covering 23, 46 and 31% of the sample

Standard errors for the treatment effect parameters are bootstrapped with 500 stratified replications, preserving the original numbers of males and females in the main sample and in the sample of older cohorts
Standard deviations of the 9th grade test score distributions are 1.5 (math), 1.2 (Danish), 1.8 (English) and 1.6 (science)

claims.statement: OLS: completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education is associated with higher in earnings at age 28 for males, conditional on the full set of controls.

treatment.label: Completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education (by age 25)

definition.value: Treatment dummy equal to one (zero) if a vocational (general) upper secondary education was completed by age 25; students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25 are categorized by their first completed program. The analysis is conditional on completing some upper secondary program.

timing.value: Completion measured by age 25; the underlying educational choice is made when students leave lower secondary school, typically at age 15 or 16

definition.value: Earnings at age 28, i.e. in the year in which the student was 28 at the beginning of the year; measured as annual wage income plus income from self-employment (before taxes), deflated by the consumer price index (base year 2015) and measured in USD 1,000 ($1 = DKK 6.5, exchange rate end of 2018). Observations are trimmed if earnings at age 28 are negative or above DKK 1m ($153,800).

timing.value: Age 28 (the year in which the person was 28 at the beginning of the year)

units.value: $1,000 of annual earnings (USD, CPI-deflated to 2015 prices)

magnitude.interpretation: Males’ earnings increase by about $7,200

estimand.target_population: Males in the main sample

population.description: Males in the main sample: individuals from the 1986-89 birth cohorts who were enrolled in Danish lower secondary schools, who had completed an upper secondary education program by age 25, who were living in Denmark the year they left lower secondary school and also at age 25 and in the years in which outcomes are measured, and for whom information on distance to educational institutions is available.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 28 (cohorts can be followed to age 28-31); predicted earnings at age 40
population.period: 9th grade typically completed in 2002-2005; registers followed until 2018
subgroups_defined: low / medium / high 9th grade math score (average of the math test score and the teacher's mark: <=7, 7-9, >=9; 23, 46 and 31% of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on having completed an upper secondary education program by age 25 (94% of the cohorts had enrolled in an upper secondary program by age 25, but only about 82% of those enrolled had completed a degree by age 25, and dropout rates are especially high in vocational programs); on residence in Denmark in the year of leaving lower secondary school, at age 25 and in the outcome years; and on having information on distance to educational institutions (students living on small islands without a bridge to the mainland are excluded).

identification.source_of_variation: Observational variation in which type of upper secondary program was completed, conditional on 3 cohort dummies, 92 municipality of residence dummies and 62 family background and 9th grade test score variables. No exogenous variation is used; the paper reports these OLS estimates as a benchmark before the MTE analysis.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the full set of controls (3 cohort dummies, 92 municipality dummies and 62 family background and 9th grade test score variables), completing a vocational rather than a general program is independent of potential earnings (selection on observables).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper offers no support and in fact argues against it: it states that the choice of program is highly endogenous, that the OLS results are very sensitive to the set of controls, especially academic ability, and that this reflects the endogeneity of educational choice.

threats_discussed: The choice of program is highly endogenous and constant effects cannot be assumed
Validity of the exclusion restriction for the distance instruments

The exclusion restriction may be more problematic for the enrollment margin than for the completion margin, because distance significantly predicts the type of education completed conditional on enrollment
Small, insignificant differences in the first-stage distance coefficients when test-score controls are excluded might be suggestive of some endogeneity of the instruments
Surrogacy and comparability assumptions behind predicted earnings at age 40 cannot be tested
Main and 'old' samples are different birth cohorts (1986-89 vs 1974-77), so comparability cannot be expected to hold exactly
Sample is conditional on having completed an upper secondary program by age 25; dropout rates are especially high in vocational programs
robustness_checks: Alternative specifications for the distance instruments (Online Appendix C.1 and C.4)
Parsimonious first-stage specification without the distance x math-score cross terms (Table 5, Columns 2 and 4)
Total income instead of earnings as the outcome at age 28 (Online Appendix C.2)
Varying the older cohorts included in the sample used to construct predicted earnings at age 40, and excluding lags of the short-term outcomes (Online Appendix C.3)
Plausibility check of surrogacy: earnings at age 28 treated as a pseudo-unobserved outcome and predicted from lagged surrogates, then compared with observed earnings at age 28 (Online Appendix C.3)
Alternative treatment definition: enrollment in (rather than completion of) vocational instead of general education
Check that the distance instruments do not significantly predict selection into the estimation sample of completers or enrollees (Online Appendix C.5)
Check that the distance instruments do not affect GPA in general upper secondary school
Placebo test: the instruments do not predict completion of compulsory (lower secondary) school
First-stage models estimated excluding controls for test scores, to gauge sensitivity of the instrument coefficients to ability controls
Excluding individuals enrolled in education at age 28 (and at ages 26 and 27) from the earnings-at-28 analysis (Online Appendix Table A14)
Alternative policy simulation setting the distance to general schools equal to the distance to vocational schools where the former is shorter (results not shown)
unresolved_confounders: Possible endogeneity of the distance instruments due to student-ability controls that are not in the data ('they might be suggestive of some endogeneity of the instruments, which should give rise to some caution when interpreting results', p. 38)
The surrogacy and comparability assumptions underlying predicted earnings at age 40 cannot be tested
Selection on unobservables: the paper states the choice of program is highly endogenous and that OLS estimates are very sensitive to the ability controls

ambiguities: The paper labels these 'OLS estimates of effects' and compares their signs directly with the MTE-based ATE, so estimand.type is recorded as ATE; the authors nevertheless state that educational choice is endogenous, so the OLS coefficient is unlikely to identify an ATE.

evidence.how: The cell carries '***' and the table legend reads '+ p < 0.10, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001', so the p-value is below 0.001. No exact p-value is printed.

Table 1 (p. 19) prints outcome means by gender and type of completed upper secondary education; the untreated state in this paper is completing a general program, so the control mean is the 'General' column for this gender and outcome.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Additional outcomes at age 28 -- employment probability, hours worked, hourly wage rate, educational attainment and fertility -- are estimated but reported only in the Online Appendix (Tables A7-A14), not in the main paper

Details of the OLS regressions used to construct predicted earnings at age 40: 'For brevity we do not report details of these regressions, but they are available on request' (footnote 11, p. 18)
An alternative PRTE policy simulation (setting distance to general schools equal to distance to vocational schools where the former is shorter): 'results not shown' (footnote 23, p. 33)
Distance squared and interactions between distance and other controls were considered but 'these terms were not significant' and are not reported (p. 25)

definition.value: Predicted ('surrogate index') earnings at age 40, in USD 1,000. key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed to avoid requiring full common support of the propensity score for all values of X; the paper follows Brinch, Mogstad and Wiswall (2017) and Cornelissen et al. (2018).

treatment.label: Completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education (by age 25)

definition.value: Treatment dummy equal to one (zero) if a vocational (general) upper secondary education was completed by age 25; students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25 are categorized by their first completed program. timing.value: Completion measured by age 25; the underlying educational choice is made when students leave lower secondary school, typically at age 15 or 16

definition.value: Predicted ('surrogate index') earnings at age 40, in USD 1,000. Four OLS models with earnings at age 40 as dependent variable are estimated on register data for older cohorts born 1974-1977, conditioning on educational attainment (290 indicators), labor market status and earnings by age 28, 29, 30 and 31 respectively (plus lags, interactions, GPA, gender, parental earnings and education; about 890 parameters, ~260,000 observations, adjusted R-squared 0.43-0.50); the coefficients are then used to predict earnings at age 40 for the 1989, 1988, 1987 and 1986 cohorts of the main sample.

timing.value: Age 40, not observed in the main sample but predicted from short-term outcomes measured by age 28-31

units.value: $1,000 of annual earnings (USD, CPI-deflated to 2015 prices)

magnitude.interpretation: By completing vocational instead of general education, males gain on average $8,000 in earnings at age 28 but lose $8,700 at age 40. Females lose $6,700 in earnings at age 28 and $12,200 at age 40.

identification.source_of_variation: Geographic variation in the weighted average road-network distances from the student's residence at about age 15 to general and to vocational upper secondary institutions (and, in the main specification, their interactions with the 9th grade math test score), conditional on cohort and 92 municipality of residence dummies, 9th grade test scores and family background. definition.value: Predicted ('surrogate index') earnings at age 40, in USD 1,000. population.period: 9th grade typically completed in 2002-2005; registers followed until 2018
subgroups_defined: low / medium / high 9th grade math score (average of the math test score and the teacher's mark: <=7, 7-9, >=9; 23, 46 and 31% of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on having completed an upper secondary education program by age 25 (94% of the cohorts had enrolled in an upper secondary program by age 25, but only about 82% of those enrolled had completed a degree by age 25, and dropout rates are especially high in vocational programs); on residence in Denmark in the year of leaving lower secondary school, at age 25 and in the outcome years; and on having information on distance to educational institutions (students living on small islands without a bridge to the mainland are excluded).

identification.source_of_variation: Geographic variation in the weighted average road-network distances from the student's residence at about age 15 to general and to vocational upper secondary institutions (and, in the main specification, their interactions with the 9th grade math test score), conditional on cohort and 92 municipality of residence dummies, 9th grade test scores and family background. Marginal treatment effects are estimated by a local-IV / control-function approach.
identification.instrument: Distance to vocational education (km), distance to general education (km), and their cross terms with the 9th grade math test score and an indicator for missing math test score

claims.statement: MTE model: the effect of completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education on predicted earnings at age 40 for females, as measured by the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), is positive and statistically significant (8.138 thousand USD).

treatment.label: Completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education (by age 25)

definition.value: Treatment dummy equal to one (zero) if a vocational (general) upper secondary education was completed by age 25; students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25 are categorized by their first completed program. The analysis is conditional on completing some upper secondary program.

timing.value: Completion measured by age 25; the underlying educational choice is made when students leave lower secondary school, typically at age 15 or 16

definition.value: Predicted ('surrogate index') earnings at age 40, in USD 1,000. Four OLS models with earnings at age 40 as dependent variable are estimated on register data for older cohorts born 1974-1977, conditioning on educational attainment (290 indicators), labor market status and earnings by age 28, 29, 30 and 31 respectively (plus lags, interactions, GPA, gender, parental earnings and education; about 890 parameters, ~260,000 observations, adjusted R-squared 0.43-0.50); the coefficients are then used to predict earnings at age 40 for the 1989, 1988, 1987 and 1986 cohorts of the main sample.

timing.value: Age 40, not observed in the main sample but predicted from short-term outcomes measured by age 28-31

units.value: $1,000 of annual earnings (USD, CPI-deflated to 2015 prices)

magnitude.interpretation: For predicted earnings at age 40, the ATT and ATUT estimates are $3,700 and -$17,300 for males, and $8,100 and -$18,100 for females.

population.description: Females in the main sample: individuals from the 1986-89 birth cohorts who were enrolled in Danish lower secondary schools, who had completed an upper secondary education program by age 25, who were living in Denmark the year they left lower secondary school and also at age 25 and in the years in which outcomes are measured, and for whom information on distance to educational institutions is available.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 28 (cohorts can be followed to age 28-31); predicted earnings at age 40
population.period: 9th grade typically completed in 2002-2005; registers followed until 2018
subgroups_defined: low / medium / high 9th grade math score (average of the math test score and the teacher's mark: <=7, 7-9, >=9; 23, 46 and 31% of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on having completed an upper secondary education program by age 25 (94% of the cohorts had enrolled in an upper secondary program by age 25, but only about 82% of those enrolled had completed a degree by age 25, and dropout rates are especially high in vocational programs); on residence in Denmark in the year of leaving lower secondary school, at age 25 and in the outcome years; and on having information on distance to educational institutions (students living on small islands without a bridge to the mainland are excluded).

identification.source_of_variation: Geographic variation in the weighted average road-network distances from the student's residence at about age 15 to general and to vocational upper secondary institutions (and, in the main specification, their interactions with the 9th grade math test score), conditional on cohort and 92 municipality of residence dummies, 9th grade test scores and family background. Marginal treatment effects are estimated by a local-IV / control-function approach.
identification.instrument: Distance to vocational education (km), distance to general education (km), and their cross terms with the 9th grade math test score and an indicator for missing math test score

claims.statement: MTE model: the effect of completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education on earnings at age 28 for males, as measured by the policy-relevant treatment effect of increasing the distance to general schools by 1 km for everyone (PRTE: Distance general + 1 km), is positive and statistically significant (9.343 thousand USD).

treatment.label: Completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education (by age 25)

definition.value: Treatment dummy equal to one (zero) if a vocational (general) upper secondary education was completed by age 25; students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25 are categorized by their first completed program. The analysis is conditional on completing some upper secondary program.

timing.value: Completion measured by age 25; the underlying educational choice is made when students leave lower secondary school, typically at age 15 or 16

definition.value: Earnings at age 28, i.e. in the year in which the student was 28 at the beginning of the year; measured as annual wage income plus income from self-employment (before taxes), deflated by the consumer price index (base year 2015) and measured in USD 1,000 ($1 = DKK 6.5, exchange rate end of 2018). Observations are trimmed if earnings at age 28 are negative or above DKK 1m ($153,800).

units.value: $1,000 of annual earnings (USD, CPI-deflated to 2015 prices)

magnitude.interpretation: effects on earnings at age 28 (of $9,300 and $11,000), but have negative effects on predicted earnings at age 40 (of -$5,300 and -$6,400).

claims.statement: MTE model: the effect of completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education on predicted earnings at age 40 for males, as measured by the policy-relevant treatment effect of increasing the distance to general schools by 1 km for everyone (PRTE: Distance general + 1 km), is negative and statistically significant (-5.305 thousand USD).

treatment.label: Completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education (by age 25)

definition.value: Treatment dummy equal to one (zero) if a vocational (general) upper secondary education was completed by age 25; students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25 are categorized by their first completed program. The analysis is conditional on completing some upper secondary program.

timing.value: Completion measured by age 25; the underlying educational choice is made when students leave lower secondary school, typically at age 15 or 16

definition.value: Predicted ('surrogate index') earnings at age 40, in USD 1,000. Four OLS models with earnings at age 40 as dependent variable are estimated on register data for older cohorts born 1974-1977, conditioning on educational attainment (290 indicators), labor market status and earnings by age 28, 29, 30 and 31 respectively (plus lags, interactions, GPA, gender, parental earnings and education; about 890 parameters, ~260,000 observations, adjusted R-squared 0.43-0.50); the coefficients are then used to predict earnings at age 40 for the 1989, 1988, 1987 and 1986 cohorts of the main sample.

timing.value: Age 40, not observed in the main sample but predicted from short-term outcomes measured by age 28-31

units.value: $1,000 of annual earnings (USD, CPI-deflated to 2015 prices)

magnitude.interpretation: effects on earnings at age 28 (of $9,300 and $11,000), but have negative effects on predicted earnings at age 40 (of -$5,300 and -$6,400).

estimand.target_population: males shifted into vocational education by a policy that increases the distance to general schools by 1 km for everyone (raising the propensity score by 0.4 percentage points for males and 0.2 for females on average); the effect is per net individual shifted
estimand.compliers: the net individuals shifted into vocational education when the distance to general schools rises by 1 km for everyone -- marginal students whose educational choice responds to that distance
estimand.formal_query: E[Y1 - Y0] for the stated target population, computed as a weighted integral of MTE(x, u_D) = E(Y1 - Y0 | X = x, U_D = u_D) over u_D

population.description: Males in the main sample: individuals from the 1986-89 birth cohorts who were enrolled in Danish lower secondary schools, who had completed an upper secondary education program by age 25, who were living in Denmark the year they left lower secondary school and also at age 25 and in the years in which outcomes are measured, and for whom information on distance to educational institutions is available.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 28 (cohorts can be followed to age 28-31); predicted earnings at age 40
population.period: 9th grade typically completed in 2002-2005; registers followed until 2018
subgroups_defined: low / medium / high 9th grade math score (average of the math test score and the teacher's mark: <=7, 7-9, >=9; 23, 46 and 31% of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on having completed an upper secondary education program by age 25 (94% of the cohorts had enrolled in an upper secondary program by age 25, but only about 82% of those enrolled had completed a degree by age 25, and dropout rates are especially high in vocational programs); on residence in Denmark in the year of leaving lower secondary school, at age 25 and in the outcome years; and on having information on distance to educational institutions (students living on small islands without a bridge to the mainland are excluded).

identification.source_of_variation: Geographic variation in the weighted average road-network distances from the student's residence at about age 15 to general and to vocational upper secondary institutions (and, in the main specification, their interactions with the 9th grade math test score), conditional on cohort and 92 municipality of residence dummies, 9th grade test scores and family background. Marginal treatment effects are estimated by a local-IV / control-function approach.
identification.instrument: Distance to vocational education (km), distance to general education (km), and their cross terms with the 9th grade math test score and an indicator for missing math test score

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity / latent index selection: treatment is determined by D = 1{Z*gamma >= V}, equivalently D = 1{P(Z) >= U_D} with U_D uniform on (0,1), so a change in the instrument moves everyone in the same direction.

claims.statement: MTE model: the effect of completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education on predicted earnings at age 40 for males, as measured by the policy-relevant treatment effect of raising the propensity score by 0.01 for students with low 9th grade math scores (PRTE: p + 0.01, math low), is not statistically significant (0.785 thousand USD).

treatment.label: Completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education (by age 25)

definition.value: Treatment dummy equal to one (zero) if a vocational (general) upper secondary education was completed by age 25; students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25 are categorized by their first completed program. The analysis is conditional on completing some upper secondary program.

timing.value: Completion measured by age 25; the underlying educational choice is made when students leave lower secondary school, typically at age 15 or 16

definition.value: Predicted ('surrogate index') earnings at age 40, in USD 1,000. Four OLS models with earnings at age 40 as dependent variable are estimated on register data for older cohorts born 1974-1977, conditioning on educational attainment (290 indicators), labor market status and earnings by age 28, 29, 30 and 31 respectively (plus lags, interactions, GPA, gender, parental earnings and education; about 890 parameters, ~260,000 observations, adjusted R-squared 0.43-0.50); the coefficients are then used to predict earnings at age 40 for the 1989, 1988, 1987 and 1986 cohorts of the main sample.

timing.value: Age 40, not observed in the main sample but predicted from short-term outcomes measured by age 28-31

units.value: $1,000 of annual earnings (USD, CPI-deflated to 2015 prices)

magnitude.interpretation: This is most pronounced for earnings at age 40 for which the increase in the propensity score for low-ability students results in a small insignificant PRTE, whereas the shift for high-ability students results in a large negative PRTE of -$11,400.

estimand.target_population: males with low 9th grade math scores shifted into vocational education by a policy that increases their propensity score by 0.01; the effect is per net individual shifted
estimand.compliers: marginal students with low 9th grade math scores (average of math test score and teacher's mark <= 7; 23% of the sample)
estimand.formal_query: E[Y1 - Y0] for the stated target population, computed as a weighted integral of MTE(x, u_D) = E(Y1 - Y0 | X = x, U_D = u_D) over u_D

population.description: Males in the main sample: individuals from the 1986-89 birth cohorts who were enrolled in Danish lower secondary schools, who had completed an upper secondary education program by age 25, who were living in Denmark the year they left lower secondary school and also at age 25 and in the years in which outcomes are measured, and for whom information on distance to educational institutions is available.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 28 (cohorts can be followed to age 28-31); predicted earnings at age 40
population.period: 9th grade typically completed in 2002-2005; registers followed until 2018
subgroups_defined: low / medium / high 9th grade math score (average of the math test score and the teacher's mark: <=7, 7-9, >=9; 23, 46 and 31% of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on having completed an upper secondary education program by age 25 (94% of the cohorts had enrolled in an upper secondary program by age 25, but only about 82% of those enrolled had completed a degree by age 25, and dropout rates are especially high in vocational programs); on residence in Denmark in the year of leaving lower secondary school, at age 25 and in the outcome years; and on having information on distance to educational institutions (students living on small islands without a bridge to the mainland are excluded).

identification.source_of_variation: Geographic variation in the weighted average road-network distances from the student's residence at about age 15 to general and to vocational upper secondary institutions (and, in the main specification, their interactions with the 9th grade math test score), conditional on cohort and 92 municipality of residence dummies, 9th grade test scores and family background. Marginal treatment effects are estimated by a local-IV / control-function approach.
identification.instrument: Distance to vocational education (km), distance to general education (km), and their cross terms with the 9th grade math test score and an indicator for missing math test score

treatment.label: Completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education (by age 25)

definition.value: Treatment dummy equal to one (zero) if a vocational (general) upper secondary education was completed by age 25; students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25 are categorized by their first completed program. The analysis is conditional on completing some upper secondary program.

timing.value: Completion measured by age 25; the underlying educational choice is made when students leave lower secondary school, typically at age 15 or 16

definition.value: Earnings at age 28, i.e. in the year in which the student was 28 at the beginning of the year; measured as annual wage income plus income from self-employment (before taxes), deflated by the consumer price index (base year 2015) and measured in USD 1,000 ($1 = DKK 6.5, exchange rate end of 2018). Observations are trimmed if earnings at age 28 are negative or above DKK 1m ($153,800).

timing.value: Age 28 (the year in which the person was 28 at the beginning of the year)

units.value: $1,000 of annual earnings (USD, CPI-deflated to 2015 prices)

magnitude.interpretation: Effects for females are mostly insignificant and there is no clear pattern.

estimand.target_population: females with low 9th grade math scores shifted into vocational education by a policy that increases their propensity score by 0.01; the effect is per net individual shifted
estimand.compliers: marginal students with low 9th grade math scores (average of math test score and teacher's mark <= 7; 23% of the sample)
estimand.formal_query: E[Y1 - Y0] for the stated target population, computed as a weighted integral of MTE(x, u_D) = E(Y1 - Y0 | X = x, U_D = u_D) over u_D

population.description: Females in the main sample: individuals from the 1986-89 birth cohorts who were enrolled in Danish lower secondary schools, who had completed an upper secondary education program by age 25, who were living in Denmark the year they left lower secondary school and also at age 25 and in the years in which outcomes are measured, and for whom information on distance to educational institutions is available.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 28 (cohorts can be followed to age 28-31); predicted earnings at age 40
population.period: 9th grade typically completed in 2002-2005; registers followed until 2018
subgroups_defined: low / medium / high 9th grade math score (average of the math test score and the teacher's mark: <=7, 7-9, >=9; 23, 46 and 31% of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on having completed an upper secondary education program by age 25 (94% of the cohorts had enrolled in an upper secondary program by age 25, but only about 82% of those enrolled had completed a degree by age 25, and dropout rates are especially high in vocational programs); on residence in Denmark in the year of leaving lower secondary school, at age 25 and in the outcome years; and on having information on distance to educational institutions (students living on small islands without a bridge to the mainland are excluded).

identification.source_of_variation: Geographic variation in the weighted average road-network distances from the student's residence at about age 15 to general and to vocational upper secondary institutions (and, in the main specification, their interactions with the 9th grade math test score), conditional on cohort and 92 municipality of residence dummies, 9th grade test scores and family background. Marginal treatment effects are estimated by a local-IV / control-function approach.
identification.instrument: Distance to vocational education (km), distance to general education (km), and their cross terms with the 9th grade math test score and an indicator for missing math test score

Validity of the exclusion restriction for the distance instruments

The exclusion restriction may be more problematic for the enrollment margin than for the completion margin, because distance significantly predicts the type of education completed conditional on enrollment
Small, insignificant differences in the first-stage distance coefficients when test-score controls are excluded might be suggestive of some endogeneity of the instruments

estimand.type is recorded as 'other' because the schema has no code for a policy-relevant treatment effect (PRTE).

evidence.how: Table 1 (p. 19) prints outcome means by gender and type of completed upper secondary education; the untreated state in this paper is completing a general program, so the control mean is the 'General' column for this gender and outcome.

value.lhs: MTE(x, p) = E(Y1 - Y0 | X = x, U_D = p)
value.parameter_of_interest: beta_1 - beta_0 and k(p); the reported ATE, ATT, ATUT and PRTE are weighted integrals of MTE(x, p)

index_sets.over: treatment states j = 0 (general) and j = 1 (vocational)
unobserved resistance to treatment U_D, uniform on (0,1)

value.normalisation: The untreated state (D = 0) is completing a general upper secondary program; U_D is uniform on (0,1) by construction; the MTE curve is evaluated at the sample means of the covariates X; ATT is evaluated at the covariate means of the treated and ATUT at those of the untreated; k_j(p) is approximated by a polynomial in the propensity score of order 2 (males age 28), 1 (males age 40), 2 (females age 28) and 3 (females age 40).
value.link_function: identity in the outcome equations; logit for the first-step propensity score P(Z)

value.claimed_domain: students at the margin of indifference between vocational and general upper secondary education in Denmark, under the specific stylized policy simulations considered
boundary_conditions: Different policies will affect different marginal groups

treatment.label: Completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education (by age 25)

definition.value: Treatment dummy equal to one (zero) if a vocational (general) upper secondary education was completed by age 25; students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25 are categorized by their first completed program. definition.value: Earnings at age 28, i.e. in the year in which the student was 28 at the beginning of the year; measured as annual wage income plus income from self-employment (before taxes), deflated by the consumer price index (base year 2015) and measured in USD 1,000 ($1 = DKK 6.5, exchange rate end of 2018). anchor_quote.text: For males, a policy increasing the propensity to complete vocational education for students with low math skills tends to have more positive effects on earnings than a policy which increases the propensity score for students with high math …

claims.statement: MTE model: the effect of completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education on predicted earnings at age 40 for females, as measured by the policy-relevant treatment effect of raising the propensity score by 0.01 for students with high 9th grade math scores (PRTE: p + 0.01, math high), is not statistically significant (0.019 thousand USD).

treatment.label: Completing a vocational instead of a general upper secondary education (by age 25)

definition.value: Treatment dummy equal to one (zero) if a vocational (general) upper secondary education was completed by age 25; students who completed both a general and a vocational program before age 25 are categorized by their first completed program. The analysis is conditional on completing some upper secondary program.

timing.value: Completion measured by age 25; the underlying educational choice is made when students leave lower secondary school, typically at age 15 or 16

definition.value: Predicted ('surrogate index') earnings at age 40, in USD 1,000. Four OLS models with earnings at age 40 as dependent variable are estimated on register data for older cohorts born 1974-1977, conditioning on educational attainment (290 indicators), labor market status and earnings by age 28, 29, 30 and 31 respectively (plus lags, interactions, GPA, gender, parental earnings and education; about 890 parameters, ~260,000 observations, adjusted R-squared 0.43-0.50); the coefficients are then used to predict earnings at age 40 for the 1989, 1988, 1987 and 1986 cohorts of the main sample.

timing.value: Age 40, not observed in the main sample but predicted from short-term outcomes measured by age 28-31

units.value: $1,000 of annual earnings (USD, CPI-deflated to 2015 prices)

magnitude.interpretation: Effects for females are mostly insignificant and there is no clear pattern.

definition.value: Equation 2 rewritten as D = 1{P(Z) >= U_D}, where P(Z) is the propensity score and U_D represents the quantiles of the unobservable V; by construction U_D is distributed uniformly over the interval (0,1) and is interpreted as unobserved resistance to treatment.

outcome.label: Marginal treatment effect (MTE) on earnings at age 28 ($1,000), males

definition.value: MTE(X = x, U_D = p) = E(Y1 - Y0 | X = x, U_D = p), the mean effect of completing vocational instead of general upper secondary education for persons at the margin of indifference with propensity score P(Z) = p; estimated from Equation 4 and evaluated at the sample means of the covariates X. The underlying earnings outcome is Earnings at age 28, i.e. in the year in which the student was 28 at the beginning of the year; measured as annual wage income plus income from self-employment (before taxes), deflated by the consumer price index (base year 2015) and measured in USD 1,000 ($1 = DKK 6.5, exchange rate end of 2018). Observations are trimmed if earnings at age 28 are negative or above DKK 1m ($153,800).

magnitude.interpretation: The MTE curve tends to be U-shaped for earnings at age 28 for males. This is not necessarily inconsistent with individuals selecting into treatment based on gains.

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity / latent index selection: treatment is determined by D = 1{Z*gamma >= V}, equivalently D = 1{P(Z) >= U_D} with U_D uniform on (0,1), so a change in the instrument moves everyone in the same direction.
Separability: E(U_j | V, X) = E(U_j | V) for j = 0,1, so that the shape of the MTE curve in U_D does not depend on X except through the intercept.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed to avoid requiring full common support of the propensity score for all values of X; the paper follows Brinch, Mogstad and Wiswall (2017) and Cornelissen et al. (2018).

claims.statement: The treatment effect on predicted earnings at age 40 for females varies significantly with observed pre-treatment covariates: the test that beta_1 - beta_0 = 0 for all covariates gives p < 0.0001.

treatment.label: Observed pre-treatment covariates X (through the difference in their coefficients across treatment states, beta_1 - beta_0)

definition.value: The vector X of control variables -- cohort and municipality dummies, 9th grade test scores and teachers' marks, family structure, ethnicity, and parental education, income, labor market status and crime -- enters the two potential-outcome equations Y_j = X*beta_j + U_j with separate coefficients, so x(beta_1 - beta_0) shifts the intercept of the MTE curve.

timing.value: Pre-treatment: measured before or at the end of lower secondary school (9th grade, about age 16)

outcome.label: Marginal treatment effect (MTE) on predicted earnings at age 40 ($1,000), females

definition.value: MTE(X = x, U_D = p) = E(Y1 - Y0 | X = x, U_D = p), the mean effect of completing vocational instead of general upper secondary education for persons at the margin of indifference with propensity score P(Z) = p; estimated from Equation 4 and evaluated at the sample means of the covariates X. The underlying earnings outcome is Predicted ('surrogate index') earnings at age 40, in USD 1,000. Four OLS models with earnings at age 40 as dependent variable are estimated on register data for older cohorts born 1974-1977, conditioning on educational attainment (290 indicators), labor market status and earnings by age 28, 29, 30 and 31 respectively (plus lags, interactions, GPA, gender, parental earnings and education; about 890 parameters, ~260,000 observations, adjusted R-squared 0.43-0.50); the coefficients are then used to predict earnings at age 40 for the 1989, 1988, 1987 and 1986 cohorts of the main sample.

timing.value: Age 40 (predicted)

magnitude.interpretation: We find important heterogeneity in effects (in terms of both observables and unobservables) that are consistent with selection on gains.

estimand.target_population: Females in the main sample; the MTE curve is evaluated at the overall sample means of the covariates
estimand.compliers: persons at the margin of indifference between vocational and general education at each value of U_D, i.e. with propensity score P(Z) = p
estimand.formal_query: variation in MTE(x, p) = E(Y1 - Y0 | X = x, U_D = p) across x

population.description: Females in the main sample: individuals from the 1986-89 birth cohorts who were enrolled in Danish lower secondary schools, who had completed an upper secondary education program by age 25, who were living in Denmark the year they left lower secondary school and also at age 25 and in the years in which outcomes are measured, and for whom information on distance to educational institutions is available.
population.ages: outcomes measured at age 28 (cohorts can be followed to age 28-31); predicted earnings at age 40
population.period: 9th grade typically completed in 2002-2005; registers followed until 2018
subgroups_defined: low / medium / high 9th grade math score (average of the math test score and the teacher's mark: <=7, 7-9, >=9; 23, 46 and 31% of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on having completed an upper secondary education program by age 25 (94% of the cohorts had enrolled in an upper secondary program by age 25, but only about 82% of those enrolled had completed a degree by age 25, and dropout rates are especially high in vocational programs); on residence in Denmark in the year of leaving lower secondary school, at age 25 and in the outcome years; and on having information on distance to educational institutions (students living on small islands without a bridge to the mainland are excluded).

identification.source_of_variation: Geographic variation in the weighted average road-network distances to general and to vocational upper secondary institutions at about age 15 (and their interactions with the 9th grade math test score), which traces out the MTE curve over the support of the propensity score.
